messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Karim's Watch

Karim was twenty-six when the accident happened. He had been working as a train conductor for three years, a job that suited him—structured, responsible, the kind of work that let him move through the day with purpose. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, his eastbound regional service was pulling into the station at New Haven when he noticed something on the tracks ahead. A man had collapsed between the rails. There was no time to stop. Karim watched from the cabin as the train rolled forward, felt the subtle lurch beneath him, heard nothing—which was somehow worse than a sound. When the emergency response teams arrived, he saw the man's leg, severed at the knee, the tourniquet of blood already darkening the platform concrete. He saw the man's face, conscious and screaming. He saw the blood on the paramedics' gloves, the spreading stain across the platform, the way the man's remaining foot twitched in shock. The company gave him two weeks off. His supervisor called it an accident, unavoidable, not his fault. But Karim had come to believe that safety was a fiction people told themselves, and that belief had calcified in him like a stone.

The months that followed unfolded quietly at first. Karim returned to work because he needed the income, because he was ashamed to admit how much that afternoon had fractured something in him. But the job had changed. Every time he sat in the conductor's cabin, he found himself scanning the tracks obsessively, looking for figures, for movement, for any sign of the chaos that could happen in an instant. His hands would go cold—sometimes just from gripping the controls, but often from a sudden awareness of his own skin, the texture of his palms against the metal, and he would think of the paramedic's gloved hand, slick and dark. He began to dread certain routes. The New Haven line was impossible; he requested reassignment, which his supervisor granted without comment. But even on different lines, he remained taut with vigilance. If he saw someone standing near the platform, his chest would tighten. If he caught sight of a wound on a passenger—a bandaged hand, a scraped knee—his mind would flood with the image of the severed leg, and he would have to look away, which only made him feel more exposed, more certain that he had missed something, that danger was everywhere.

At night, sleep became a negotiation with his own mind. Karim would lie in his apartment and feel his heart rate climb as darkness settled. He had come to believe that sleep was a luxury he could not afford, that the moment he closed his eyes, something would happen—not necessarily to him, but around him, and he would miss it, fail to see it coming. So he stayed awake, or half-awake, his body rigid, listening to the sounds of the building, the street, the world outside his window. By two in the morning he would still be conscious, alert, waiting. When he finally did sleep, it was shallow and fractured, and he would wake at any small sound—a siren, a car door, a neighbor's footstep—his body flooded with adrenaline.

The triggers that had seized him in those early months never loosened their grip. A passenger's cough would make him look up sharply. The sight of someone's bleeding lip in a coffee shop would send a spike of fear through his chest, and he would find himself unable to finish his coffee, would leave money on the table and walk out. What terrified him most was that these moments were unpredictable. He could not prepare for them. He could only remain vigilant, scanning, waiting. Even when his sister called to reassure him that he was safe, that the accident was not his fault, that thousands of trains ran without incident every day, he could not believe her. The reassurance felt hollow, a kind of denial of the truth he had learned: that catastrophe lived in the ordinary world, and that no amount of caution or watching could keep it at bay. The temperature of his own skin—a flush of heat, a sudden chill—would remind him of the paramedic's gloved hand, and then the hypervigilance would spike again, his shoulders tensing, his breath shallow. Three years had passed since the accident, and Karim had become a man who could not trust that anything was truly safe, who had learned to live in a state of constant readiness, who had begun to understand that the price of that readiness was isolation and exhaustion.

It was his supervisor's gentle insistence that finally brought him to a therapist's office. Karim had missed more shifts, called in sick more often, and his performance had declined. He was not sleeping. He was afraid of his own job. And though he could not articulate it clearly, he was beginning to understand that whatever had broken in him that afternoon in March was not going to heal on its own.
